gap_description.what_is_missing:
Three distinct explainability gaps are present in the submission for this P6 control:

1. **No contestability mechanism beyond adverse notice**: There is no documented process or channel enabling adversely affected applicants to formally challenge or contest AI-generated outputs. Receipt of an adverse action notice alone does not satisfy OECD Principle 1.30(iv), which requires a meaningful right to contest.

2. **No audit or monitoring regime for explainability outputs**: There is no documentation describing how SHAP attributions or other explainability outputs are reviewed over time for accuracy, consistency, or drift. Without this, degradation in explanation quality (e.g., due to model updates or data distribution shift) would go undetected.

3. **No communication of system limitations or uncertainty**: Neither the technical documentation nor user-facing materials reference how the system conveys its confidence levels, known limitations, or uncertainty to either technical reviewers or end users, as required by NIST AI RMF 3.5 and OECD transparency principles.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **Contestability mechanism**: Design and document a formal recourse workflow that allows adversely affected applicants to lodge a challenge against an AI-driven decision. This should include: a named intake channel (e.g., dedicated email, portal form), defined SLA for response, escalation path to a human reviewer with authority to override, and a record-keeping process for all challenges and outcomes. Update the adverse action notice template to explicitly reference this channel.

2. **Explainability monitoring and audit**: Establish a recurring audit schedule (e.g., quarterly) for SHAP attribution outputs. Document the methodology for detecting attribution drift — including baseline benchmarks, statistical thresholds for flagging anomalies, and the roles responsible for review. Produce and retain audit logs and summary reports from each review cycle. Integrate explainability drift checks into the existing model monitoring pipeline.

3. **Uncertainty and limitations communication**: Draft and implement standardised language — calibrated separately for technical audiences (e.g., model cards, internal dashboards) and end users (e.g., plain-language disclosures in notices or portals) — that conveys confidence levels, known model limitations, and conditions under which outputs should be treated with additional caution. Reference NIST AI RMF 3.5 and OECD transparency principles explicitly in the supporting policy documentation.

SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.1.03
Title: Central Function: Risk Assessment and Monitoring

The government has established a central function within DSIT with multiple activities: (1) Risk assessment - recruited new multidisciplinary team to undertake cross-sectoral risk monitoring, bringing together expertise in risk, regulation, and AI with backgrounds in data science, engineering, economics, and law. This team will provide continuous examination of cross-cutting AI risks, including evaluating effectiveness of interventions by government and regulators. In 2024, targeted consultation on a cross-economy AI risk register will be launched to ensure it comprehensively captures range of risks. The register will provide single source of truth on AI risks for regulators, government departments, and external groups. It will support identifying risks that fall across or between regulator remits to identify gaps or where existing regulation is ineffective. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities. TITLE: Technical documentation

Providers of high-risk AI systems shall draw up technical documentation that demonstrates compliance with the requirements of this Regulation. The technical documentation shall include a general description of the AI system, the intended purpose, the training and testing procedures used.

gap_description.actionable_suggestion:

Cross-reference it explicitly from the model card.

2. **Expand technical documentation for training & testing**: Augment the model card and/or a supplementary technical document to include: (a) full data preprocessing pipeline steps, (b) train/validation/test split rationale and composition, (c) validation methodology (e.g., cross-validation strategy, holdout approach), and (d) test set characteristics and representativeness — all mapped explicitly to EU AI Act Article 11 requirements.

Title: Executive Summary: AI Safety Institute Establishment

The AI Safety Institute was created to lead evaluations and safety research in UK government, in collaboration with international partners including the US. At the AI Safety Summit, leading AI developers committed to sharing the most powerful AI models with governments for testing to ensure safety today and prepare for risks of tomorrow. The Institute will conduct pre- and post-deployment testing of the most powerful AI systems, performing evaluations to characterize safety-relevant capabilities, understand safety and security of systems, and assess societal impacts. SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 19
TITLE: Bias monitoring and mitigation

Providers and users of high-risk AI systems shall implement measures to monitor, detect and mitigate bias. Training data shall be tested to identify potential biases and documented methods for bias mitigation shall be in place. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Executive Summary
SECTION: Executive Summary
TOPIC: This chunk introduces the dual nature of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, highlighting their transformative potential alongside the diverse risks they pose, and provides a foundational definition of an AI system.
---
Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies possess immense potential to profoundly transform society and individuals' lives across various sectors, including commerce, health, transportation, cybersecurity, and environmental management. These technologies are capable of driving inclusive economic growth and fostering scientific advancements that contribute to improving global conditions. However, alongside these significant benefits, AI technologies also introduce a range of risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, communities, society, the environment, and the planet. These AI-related risks can manifest in diverse ways, characterized by their duration (long- or short-term), likelihood (high- or low-probability), scope (systemic or localized), and severity of impact (high- or low-impact).
Within the context of the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), an "AI system" is specifically defined as an engineered or machine-based system. The core capability of such a system is to generate outputs, such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions, for a given set of objectives. These outputs are designed to influence either real or virtual environments. Furthermore, AI systems are developed to operate with varying degrees of autonomy, meaning their ability to function independently can differ significantly based on their design and purpose. This definition is adapted from established international sources, including the OECD Recommendation on AI (2019) and ISO/IEC 22989:2022, providing a consistent understanding for risk management purposes.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Four distinct deficiencies exist under the AI identity non-deception control (P6):

1. **Edge-case policy gap**: No explicit policy or procedure documents how staff must handle situations where the AI system's identity or nature could be misrepresented during verbal or informal communications with applicants. The submission references general policies but provides no specific guidance for these scenarios.

2. **Staff training gap**: No staff training programme, awareness measures, or competency verification is described to ensure all personnel consistently and accurately represent the AI system's nature to applicants. Without this, policy intent cannot be reliably operationalised.

3. **Audit and monitoring gap**: No mechanism is described to verify that disclosures on forms, notices, or other applicant-facing materials remain accurate and up-to-date over time — particularly following system updates, model changes, or scope changes that could render existing disclosures misleading.

4. **Future-scope gap**: No forward-looking procedure or trigger-based review process is referenced to ensure AI identity non-deception obligations are re-evaluated and maintained if the system's scope expands to include direct applicant-facing interactions (e.g., chatbots, automated decision notices, or real-time AI-assisted communications).
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **Edge-case policy**: Draft and formally approve a supplementary procedure (as an annex to the existing AI policy) that explicitly covers verbal and informal staff-to-applicant communications. This must define prohibited misrepresentations, escalation paths, and consequences for non-compliance. Assign a named owner and approval date.

2. **Staff training**: Design and deliver a targeted training module on AI identity non-deception for all staff who interact with applicants or handle AI-related disclosures. Record completion rates and assessment outcomes. Ensure training is refreshed at least annually and upon material system changes.

3. **Audit and monitoring mechanism**: Implement a documented review cycle (recommended: at minimum annually and triggered by any system update) to verify the accuracy of all applicant-facing disclosures. Define who is responsible for initiating reviews, what artefacts are reviewed, and how findings are tracked to resolution. Retain logs of each review cycle.

4. **Future-scope trigger process**: Document a formal change-management trigger that mandates a P6 non-deception re-assessment whenever the system's scope is proposed to expand to applicant-facing interactions. Embed this trigger within the organisation's existing change management or AI governance framework and reference it explicitly in the AI identity non-deception policy.

SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 1.7
Title: Safe Systems: Data Quality and Relevance

Data used as part of any automated system's creation, evaluation, or deployment should be relevant, of high quality, and tailored to the task at hand. Relevancy should be established based on research-backed demonstration of the causal influence of the data to the specific use case. High quality and tailored data should be representative of the task at hand and errors from data entry or other sources should be measured and limited. Any data used as the target of a prediction process should receive particular attention to the quality and validity of the predicted outcome or label. Justification should be documented for each data attribute and source. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.02
Title: Highly Capable AI: Life Cycle Accountability Gaps

Many of UK's current legal frameworks and regulator remits may not effectively mitigate risks posed by highly capable general-purpose AI systems. Many regulators in UK can struggle to enforce existing rules on those actors designing, training, and developing most powerful general-purpose AI systems. It is not always clear how existing rules can be applied to effectively address risks that highly capable general-purpose models can present. Existing rules and laws are frequently applied to deployment or application level of AI, but organizations deploying or using these systems may not be well placed to identify, assess, or mitigate risks they can present. If this is case, new responsibilities on developers of highly capable general-purpose models may more effectively address risks. The government's ongoing work analysing life cycle accountability for AI may eventually need to consider role of other actors across value chain, such as data or cloud hosting providers, to determine how legal responsibility for AI may be distributed most fairly and effectively.
